title: Absolute normalization of a trait and local lifting of scheme points
statement: Let $R$ be a discrete valuation ring [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring], $K$ its fraction field, $\overline K$ an algebraic closure [def-weil-algebraic-closure], and $\pi$ a uniformizer of $R$. Let $B\subseteq\overline K$ be the integral closure of $R$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure], $S=\operatorname{Spec}R$ and $T=\operatorname{Spec}B$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum]. Then $T\to S$ is flat, surjective and quasi-compact, hence fpqc [def-weil-flat-morphism, def-weil-pbc-fpqc-covering]. The generic inverse image is the open $D(\pi)=\operatorname{Spec}\overline K$; every other point $t\in T$ lies over the closed point of $S$, is closed in $T$, and has algebraically closed residue field $\kappa(t)$ [def-weil-residue-field]. If $Y\to S$ is any flat locally finite type morphism of schemes [def-pc-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism], set $Y_T=Y\times_ST$ [def-pc-fibre-product]. For every point $t\in T$ over the closed point of $S$ and every $\kappa(t)$-morphism $y:\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(t)\to Y_T$ over $T$, there exist a Zariski open neighborhood $W\subseteq T$ of $t$ and a $T$-morphism $\sigma:W\to Y_T$ whose restriction at $t$ is $y$. The ring $B$ need not be Noetherian, and $Y$ need not be quasi-compact.

source.place: Tag 05GU, lemma-quasi-finite-quasi-section-meeting-nearby-open-X, the quasi-section input; absolute-normalization local-section consequence used in Anantharaman, 3.4.1, printed p.52, proof first paragraph (primary scan https://www.numdam.org/article/MSMF_1973__33__5_0.pdf; local archive WANTED). Algebraically closed residue fields and strict henselian localizations: more-algebra.tex Tags 0DCQ (lemma-normal-domain-absolutely-integrally-closed) and 0DCS (lemma-absolutely-integrally-closed-strictly-henselian).

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-integral-closure-algebraic-extension-normal] to $R\subset K\subset\overline K$. It gives that $B$ is a domain integral over $R$, normal, with fraction field $\overline K$. Since $B\subset\overline K$ and $R\hookrightarrow\overline K$, multiplication by every nonzero element of $R$ on $B$ is injective. The DVR is a PID by [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring], so [lem-weil-pbc-pid-torsion-free-module-flat] makes $B$ flat over $R$. By [lem-weil-pbc-flat-ring-map-iff-flat-affine], $T\to S$ is flat. Lying over [pqf-lem-lying-over] makes it surjective. The integral affine-map dictionary [lem-weil-pbc-spec-integral-ring-map-integral] and [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism] make the map affine; [lem-weil-pbc-affine-morphism-permanence] makes it quasi-compact. Thus it is fpqc: for any affine open $V\subset S$, its inverse image is affine and surjects onto $V$, which supplies the single affine open required in [def-weil-pbc-fpqc-covering].

source.place: Tags 00GO, 0308, 034L, 00GU; More on Algebra 0AUW; Morphisms 01U5, 01S7; Topologies 022B. Normalization and flatness argument.

proof.text: The DVR is Noetherian since every ideal is principal. By [lem-weil-pbc-dvr-unit-times-uniformizer-power], every nonzero $r\in R$ is $u\pi^n$, so $R[1/\pi]=K$. Every nonzero prime of $R$ contains such an $r$, hence contains $\pi$ and equals the maximal ideal. For $\alpha\in\overline K$, choose a monic relation $\alpha^d+c_1\alpha^{d-1}+\cdots+c_d=0$ over $K$. Choose $N$ with $\pi^{Ni}c_i\in R$ for every $i$. Then $\pi^N\alpha$ satisfies the monic equation with coefficients $\pi^{Ni}c_i$, so belongs to $B$. Hence $B[1/\pi]=\overline K$. The principal-open scheme description [lem-weil-pbc-principal-localization-open-immersion] now identifies $D(\pi)$ with $\operatorname{Spec}\overline K$, the full generic inverse image. Every other prime contracts to the maximal ideal of $R$ and is maximal by [lem-weil-pbc-integral-prime-over-maximal-maximal]; thus its point is closed in $T$.

source.place: Tag 00PD (lemma-characterize-dvr), Tag 00E3 (lemma-spec-localization), integral primes over maximal ideals; explicit denominator scaling of algebraic elements.

proof.text: Let $t$ be one of these closed points, with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m\subset B$. Every monic positive-degree polynomial over $B$ has a root in $\overline K$; that root is integral over $B$ and belongs to $B$ because $B$ is integrally closed in $\overline K$. A monic polynomial over $B/\mathfrak m$ lifts coefficient by coefficient to a monic polynomial over $B$, so also has a root. Since $\kappa(t)=B/\mathfrak m$ is a field, this proves that it is algebraically closed, without any perfectness assumption. Put $A=B_{\mathfrak m}$. By [lem-weil-pbc-localization-normal-domain], $A$ is normal with fraction field $\overline K$. The statement [lem-weil-pbc-gabber-quotient-localizations], with ring $B$ and ideal $0$, makes $A$ strictly henselian, in particular henselian. Its residue field is canonically $\kappa(t)$.

source.place: Tags 0DCQ, 0DCN, 0DCS (monic-polynomial argument); etale-cohomology.tex Tags 09Z9 and 09ZC for strict henselian localizations; Algebra 00GY.

proof.text: Fix the prescribed $y$ and let $x\in Y$ be its image. Choose an affine open $U=\operatorname{Spec}C\subset Y$ containing $x$. By [lem-weil-pbc-lft-affine-pairs], $C$ is of finite type over $R$, and by [lem-weil-pbc-flat-morphism-affine-criterion] it is flat. Since $R$ is Noetherian, [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-noetherian-finite-presentation] gives a finite presentation $C=R[X_1,\ldots,X_n]/(F_1,\ldots,F_r)$. The morphism $y$ supplies an $R$-algebra map $h:C\to\kappa(t)$. Write $k=R/(\pi)$. By [lem-a1-integral-residue-extension-algebraic], $\kappa(t)/k$ is algebraic. The image of $C/(\pi)$ under $h$ is generated by finitely many algebraic elements over $k$, hence is a finite-dimensional $k$-algebra which is a domain. It is a field: multiplication by a nonzero element is injective on a finite-dimensional vector space and therefore surjective. Thus $C/\ker h$ is a finite field extension of $k$, equals $\kappa(x)$, and [lem-trf-finite-residue-point-closed-in-fibre] says that $x$ is closed in $U_s$.

source.place: Tag 00FP (lemma-Noetherian-finite-type-is-finite-presentation); Morphisms 01T2, 01U5, 01TE; algebraic residue extension and the finite-dimensional image argument.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sc-flat-going-down] to the flat map $R\to C$, the primes $(0)\subset(\pi)$ and $\ker h$. We obtain a prime of $C$ contained in $\ker h$ and contracting to $(0)$. Its point $x'$ belongs to $U_\eta$ and specializes to $x$. Apply [lem-sfb-quasi-section-nearby-open] to $U\to S$, $x$ and the open $U_\eta$. Its hypotheses hold: $S$ is locally Noetherian, the morphism is locally finite type, $x$ is closed in $U_s$, and $x'$ is the required nearby point over a different base point. Obtain an integral closed subscheme $Z\subset U$ through $x$, dominant over $S$, and quasi-finite at $x$. No quasi-section theorem has been applied over $B$ or $A$.

source.place: Tag 05GU (lemma-quasi-finite-quasi-section-meeting-nearby-open-X), with Algebra Tag 00HS (lemma-flat-going-down) supplying its nearby generic point.

proof.text: By [pqf-def-quasifinite], choose an affine neighbourhood $V=\operatorname{Spec}D$ of $x$ in $Z$ such that $R\to D$ is finite type and quasi-finite at the prime $\mathfrak q$ of $x$. We may use $S$ as target affine chart, since it is local and its only open containing $s$ is $S$. The nonempty open $V$ of the integral scheme $Z$ is integral and contains its generic point; hence $D$ is a domain and $R\to D$ is injective by dominance. Consequently $D$ is torsion-free over the PID $R$, and [lem-weil-pbc-pid-torsion-free-module-flat] makes it flat. The morphism $\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(t)\to U$ factors through $Z$ because its kernel is the prime of $x$ and the ideal of $Z$ lies in that prime; it then factors through $V$ because its only point maps to $x\in V$. Denote the resulting map by $h_D:D\to\kappa(t)$; its kernel is $\mathfrak q$.

source.place: Tag 05GU, integral quasi-section construction; Morphisms Tag 01TD, affine definition of quasi-finiteness at a point; More on Algebra 0AUW.

proof.text: Form $P=A\otimes_R D$. The homomorphism $P\to\kappa(t)$ given by $a\otimes d\mapsto\bar a\,h_D(d)$ is surjective, since $A\to\kappa(t)$ is. Let $\mathfrak n$ be its kernel. Its contractions to $A$ and $D$ are $\mathfrak m_A$ and $\mathfrak q$, and its contraction to $R$ is $(\pi)$. The map $R=R_{(\pi)}\to A$ is local. Apply [lem-trf-quasi-finite-henselian-tensor-factor] with base ring $R$, finite-type algebra $D$, henselian ring $A$, and prime $\mathfrak n$. It gives that $E=P_{\mathfrak n}$ is a finite local $A$-algebra. It is nonzero because it is localization at a proper prime. The map $P\to\kappa(t)$ extends to $E$ and induces an isomorphism $E/\mathfrak m_E\cong\kappa(t)$.

source.place: Tag 04GH (lemma-finite-over-henselian), part (3); Tag 05WP (lemma-quasi-finite-henselization), proof: the quasi-finite henselian tensor factor. The canonical residue map specifies the prime.

proof.text: The localized base-change flatness statement [lem-weil-pbc-flat-localized-module-base-change], with the pushout $P=A\otimes_R D$, module $N=D$ and $M=P$, implies that $E=P_{\mathfrak n}$ is flat over $A$, since $D_{\mathfrak q}$ is a domain containing $R$, hence torsion-free and flat over the PID $R$ by [lem-weil-pbc-pid-torsion-free-module-flat]. By [lem-trf-flat-module-torsionfree-domain], $E$ is torsion-free over the domain $A$. Therefore its localization $E_{\overline K}=\overline K\otimes_AE$ is nonzero: if $1$ vanished, some nonzero $a\in A$ would annihilate $1_E$, contradicting torsion-freeness and $E\ne0$. This generic algebra is finite-dimensional over $\overline K$, because finitely many $A$-module generators of $E$ still generate after base change. Choose a maximal ideal in this nonzero algebra. By [lem-wf-affine-nullstellensatz-vanishing] (1), its residue field is $\overline K$. The quotient gives a generic section of $\operatorname{Spec}E\to\operatorname{Spec}A$.

source.place: Tag 00FV (theorem-nullstellensatz) and the finite algebra generic fibre; flat localized scalar extension and More on Algebra Tag 0539 (flat implies torsion-free).

proof.text: The scheme $\operatorname{Spec}A$ is integral with function field $\overline K$ by [lem-weil-pbc-spec-domain-stalks-function-field]. Its local rings are normal by [lem-weil-pbc-localization-normal-domain]. Since $E$ is a finitely generated $A$-module (step 7), $\operatorname{Spec}E\to\operatorname{Spec}A$ is finite [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism] by [lem-weil-pbc-spec-finite-ring-map-finite]. Apply [lem-sfb-finite-normal-generic-section-extension] to the generic section just constructed. Obtain an $A$-algebra retraction $\rho:E\to A$. Its reduction $E\to A\to\kappa(t)$ is surjective and has maximal kernel. Since $E$ is local, this kernel is $\mathfrak m_E$. Both this map and the map from step 7 induce $\kappa(t)$-algebra maps $E/\mathfrak m_E\to\kappa(t)$; the structural map $\kappa(t)\to E/\mathfrak m_E$ is an isomorphism by step 7, so these two maps coincide. Composing $C\to D\to P\to E\xrightarrow{\rho}A$ therefore gives an $R$-algebra homomorphism $g:C\to B_{\mathfrak m}$ whose residue is exactly $h$, including the specified residue-field morphism, not just its image point.

source.place: Tag 0AB1 (lemma-finite-birational-over-normal), normal-base generic-section extension; algebraic local-ring residue comparison written explicitly.

proof.text: For each of the finitely many generators $X_i$, write $g(X_i)=b_i/s_i$ with $s_i\notin\mathfrak m$. Set $f=\prod_i s_i$, with the empty product $1$. Then all generator images lie in $B[1/f]\subset B_{\mathfrak m}\subset\overline K$. Every relation $F_j(b_i/s_i)$ is zero there because it is zero in $B_{\mathfrak m}$ and $B[1/f]\hookrightarrow B_{\mathfrak m}$ is injective (both are subrings of the fraction field of the domain $B$). Thus the finite presentation in step 4 defines an $R$-algebra map $C\to B[1/f]$ inducing $g$. Contravariantly it gives a morphism $W=D(f)\to U\subset Y$ over $S$. Pair it with $W\hookrightarrow T$ to obtain $\sigma:W\to Y_T$ by the fibre-product universal property [def-pc-fibre-product]. Since $f\notin\mathfrak m$, $W$ contains $t$; the residue equality in step 9 says $\sigma|_{\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(t)}=y$. Only one affine neighbourhood of $x$ was used, so no quasi-compactness of $Y$ was required, and no finiteness or Noetherian property of $B$ was used.
